passage:
At the swimming pool in Porto, Sofia kicked her way across the whole width for the first time. She climbed out, stood tall with her chest pushed out and her hands on her hips, dripping and grinning at her mother.

"You did it!" Beatriz said.

That afternoon, at a cousin's birthday, the same girl hid behind her mother's leg, peeking out at the crowd of children.

"Go and say hello," an aunt urged.

"She'll go when she's ready," Beatriz said, and stroked her hair. Twenty minutes later Sofia was chasing balloons.

qa.q: Where did Sofia swim across the whole width for the first time?
qa.a: At the swimming pool in Porto.

qa.q: What was Sofia feeling when she stood with her chest out and hands on her hips?
qa.a: She was most likely proud of her first full width. Later, hiding behind her mother's leg shows she felt shy and wary in a crowd of children.

qa.q: Which choice worked at the birthday, and why?
qa.a: Beatriz let Sofia warm up in her own time instead of pushing her, and she joined the balloon chase once she felt ready.

qa.q: How does the aunt see Sofia's hiding compared with Beatriz?
qa.a: The aunt thinks Sofia just needs a push to say hello, while Beatriz sees a shy child who needs time.

grounding: It shows a preschooler standing tall with pride after a success and hiding behind a leg when shy, with warm-up time instead of pressure.

passage:
The music was just starting at Ayesha's birthday when the power went out. The speaker died, the fan slowed, and the room went dim.

Ayesha's face fell. Then Uma Nani started to sing and clap. Ayesha jumped up and spun in circles, arms out, skirt flying, laughing.

Her cousins joined in. Uma Nani got up from her chair and danced too, slowly, holding Ayesha's hands.

When the lights came back, nobody wanted the speaker. They kept singing until they were out of breath.

qa.q: What happened just as the music was starting?
qa.a: The power went out.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when she spun in circles with her arms out?
qa.a: She was most likely full of joy and excitement once the singing started, after a moment of disappointment when the power went. Spinning let all that energy out.

qa.q: What did Uma Nani do that helped most?
qa.a: She joined in, first singing and clapping and then dancing while holding Ayesha's hands, which turned a letdown into a shared, happy moment. 😊

qa.q: What would change if Uma Nani had only watched and said "Well done"?
qa.a: Ayesha would still enjoy dancing, but she might miss the closeness of dancing together with her Nani.

grounding: It shows a preschooler spinning and dancing for joy at her birthday and an adult joining in, which brings them closer.

passage:
Monday: Samir lost at carrom and walked straight out of the room. Bhupen Chacha followed him down the corridor. "Come back! Say good game! Don't be a bad loser!" Samir ran into the bedroom and slammed the door.

Thursday: Samir lost again and turned away. This time Chacha stayed put. "The board's here when you're ready." A few minutes later, Samir crept back and sat down.

The next Sunday: Samir lost, frowned hard at the board, and stayed. "Again," he said.

qa.q: What game did Samir lose?
qa.a: Carrom.

qa.q: What was Samir probably feeling when he walked out after losing?
qa.a: He was most likely upset and embarrassed about losing. On Monday, being followed with demands seemed to make him feel more cornered, so he slammed the door.

qa.q: What went wrong on Monday, and what fixed it later?
qa.a: Following Samir with demands pushed him further away; a calm invitation on Thursday gave him space and he came back on his own.

qa.q: How does Bhupen Chacha's approach change between Monday and Thursday?
qa.a: On Monday he chases Samir and lectures him, but on Thursday he stays put and leaves the door open for him to return.

grounding: It shows a young child walking off after losing and a calm invitation to come back working better than following with demands.

passage:
Diwali night, and the whole colony was bursting crackers at once. Jaya held Seema's hand on the balcony, but every bang made Seema flinch. Soon she pressed both hands hard over her ears and squeezed her eyes shut.

"Too loud?" Jaya bent down. Seema nodded without opening her eyes.

"Come. We'll watch from inside."

Jaya shut the balcony door and they sat in the bedroom, where the noise was only a thud. Seema lowered her hands. Through the window they watched the sky turn gold and green.

qa.q: Where did Jaya and Seema watch the sky from in the end?
qa.a: From the bedroom, through the window.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling when she pressed her hands over her ears and shut her eyes?
qa.a: She was most likely frightened and overwhelmed by the constant bangs. She still seemed to enjoy the colours once the noise was quieter.

qa.q: How did Jaya respect Seema's signal?
qa.a: She asked if it was too loud, accepted the nod, and moved her to a quieter room without telling her to be brave.

qa.q: What would change if Jaya had pulled Seema's hands off her ears?
qa.a: Seema might have become more scared and learnt that her signals don't count, instead of learning that limits are allowed.

grounding: It shows a preschooler covering her ears and eyes against loud crackers and an adult respecting it by moving to a quieter space.

passage:
Note from Tushar, school annual day, for Aditi's mother

After the dance, a visiting uncle of Aditi's came backstage and pulled her into a tight hug. Aditi went stiff, turned her face away and tried to wriggle out. He laughed and hugged her again.

I stepped in and said, "Aditi can wave or give a high-five instead." She waved. He shrugged and left.

Then I sat with Aditi. We practised saying, "No, thank you, I don't want a hug," and I told her she can always tell me or her mother if anyone keeps pushing. I am telling you today as well.

qa.q: What did the visiting uncle do after Aditi tried to wriggle out?
qa.a: He laughed and hugged her again.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she went stiff and turned her face away?
qa.a: She was most likely uncomfortable and upset about a hug she did not want, and her stiff body was a clear signal. She may also have been tired and overwhelmed after the dance.

qa.q: What did Tushar do that protected Aditi?
qa.a: Tushar stepped in with another choice, a wave or high-five, practised a clear "No, thank you" with her, reminded her she can tell a trusted adult, and informed her mother the same day.

qa.q: How might Aditi's mother feel reading the note?
qa.a: She would likely be glad Aditi's discomfort was noticed and respected, and able to follow up at home that evening.

grounding: It shows a child stiffening and pulling away from an unwanted hug, an adult respecting the signal, and the child practising saying no and telling.

subtype: Covering the mouth when shy or surprised [Expressing]
passage:
At the vegetable market near their flat, Payal stared at Nazia Aunty's new short haircut. "It looks like a broom!" she said loudly.

Then her hand flew up over her mouth. Her eyes went wide above her fingers, and her cheeks turned pink.

Nazia Aunty tilted her head and smiled. "A nice broom, I hope?"

Payal giggled behind her hand, then took it away. "A very nice broom. Sorry."

A minute later, a man tossed a whole pumpkin to the stall owner, and Payal's hand went to her mouth again, this time in pure amazement.

qa.q: What did Payal say Nazia Aunty's haircut looked like?
qa.a: A broom.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling when her hand flew over her mouth the first time?
qa.a: She was most likely embarrassed that she had blurted out something rude; her pink cheeks show it. The second time, the same gesture showed amazement at the pumpkin.

qa.q: How did Nazia Aunty help Payal feel safe after the slip?
qa.a: She smiled and joked about it, so Payal could giggle, take her hand away and say sorry without feeling scared. 🙂

qa.q: What is it like for Nazia Aunty to hear her haircut called a broom?
qa.a: It could sting a little, but she chooses to take it lightly and keeps the moment friendly.

grounding: It shows a child covering her mouth after a rude slip and again in amazement, with context showing which and a smile helping her feel safe.

passage:
The clinic waiting room was full, and their number was still far off. Nilesh chewed his thumbnail, then picked at the button on his shirt, then chewed again.

"Stop biting! How many times?" Yogesh snapped, pulling his son's hand down. Nilesh's lip trembled.

Yogesh took a breath and dug in his pocket. "Here. Squeeze this." He handed him the rubber keychain from his keys. "And let's breathe. Smell the flower... blow out the candle."

Nilesh squeezed and breathed. His hands stayed busy with the keychain until their number was called.

qa.q: What did Yogesh hand Nilesh to squeeze?
qa.a: The rubber keychain from his keys.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh keep chewing his nail and picking at his button?
qa.a: He was probably nervous about seeing the doctor and restless from the long wait, and the chewing helped soothe him. When he was snapped at, his trembling lip showed he felt hurt.

qa.q: Which choice worked better, and why?
qa.a: Giving Nilesh the keychain to squeeze and breathing with him worked better than scolding, because it gave his worried hands something calm to do.

qa.q: How does Yogesh's view of the nail biting change?
qa.a: At first he treats it as a bad habit to stop, but after taking a breath he sees it as his son's way of coping with nerves.

grounding: It shows a preschooler biting his nails and fidgeting while waiting nervously, and a squeeze toy and breathing working better than scolding.

passage:
Pickup note from Hafsa, Friday

Wasim's Nanu came to collect him today. He bent down and said, "Kiss for Nanu?" Wasim stepped back and held his school bag in front of him. Then he looked at me.

Last week we practised choices for greetings, so I said, "Wasim, you can choose." Wasim held up his hand. "High-five?"

Nanu laughed and gave him the biggest high-five. "Good one!"

Wasim walked out holding Nanu's hand, chatting all the way. Please keep offering him choices at home too.

qa.q: What did Wasim hold in front of him when he stepped back?
qa.a: His school bag.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when he stepped back and looked at Hafsa?
qa.a: He was probably unsure and a little uncomfortable about giving a kiss, and looked to Hafsa for support. Once he had a choice he seemed relieved and happy, chatting all the way out.

qa.q: Why was the high-five a good outcome?
qa.a: Wasim chose how to greet, and Nanu accepted it warmly, which teaches Wasim that his body belongs to him even with family.

qa.q: How does Nanu respond to being offered a high-five instead of a kiss?
qa.a: He laughs and gives the biggest high-five, showing he is happy to greet Wasim in the way Wasim chooses.

grounding: It shows a preschooler choosing a high-five instead of a kiss with a relative and an adult accepting it, teaching that his body belongs to him.

passage:
"Mummy, what's a safe touch?"

Bhavna put down the book from school. "A hug you want. A high-five. Holding hands to cross the road. It feels okay."

"And unsafe?"

"Touch that feels scary or confusing. And nobody touches the parts your swimming costume covers, except to keep you clean or healthy, with me there."

Naveen thought, scratching his ear. "What about tickling? When Bhaiya tickles and I say stop and he doesn't stop, I don't like it."

"Thank you for telling me, beta. When you say stop, it stops. I'll talk to Bhaiya this evening."

"And if someone says keep it secret?"

"Then you tell me, or Teacher, straight away."

qa.q: What examples of safe touch did Bhavna give?
qa.a: A hug you want, a high-five, and holding hands to cross the road.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling about Bhaiya's tickling?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and upset when the tickling carried on after he said stop, and probably a bit confused because tickling is meant to be fun.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do well when Naveen told her about the tickling?
qa.a: She thanked him, told him clearly that "stop" should be respected, and said she would speak to Bhaiya that same evening.

qa.q: How might Bhaiya see the tickling differently from Naveen?
qa.a: Bhaiya probably thinks it is just a game, without noticing that it stops feeling fun for Naveen when he says stop.

grounding: It shows a child learning that safe touch feels comfortable, unsafe touch feels confusing, private areas are protected and secrets about touch should be told.

passage:
I'm Suraj, and I sit next to Gautam in class. Gautam always stands really close when he talks, right up at your nose. Yesterday he told me about his new shoes so close I stepped back into the wall.

Teacher saw. She called us both over. "Let's try this. Stretch out your arm, Gautam. That's a good space for talking to friends."

Gautam stretched his arm, grinned, and stepped back. It looked a bit strange at first.

At home time his Nani squeezed him in a big hug, and he didn't step back at all.

qa.q: What did Gautam tell Suraj about?
qa.a: His new shoes.

qa.q: What might Gautam be feeling when he stands so close?
qa.a: He is probably excited and eager to share, not trying to crowd anyone; his grin when Teacher coached him suggests he felt fine about learning the new rule, maybe a little surprised.

qa.q: How did Teacher coach Gautam?
qa.a: She gave him a clear, simple measure, stretching out his arm, instead of scolding him, so he knew what a comfortable distance looks like.

qa.q: How does the close talking affect Suraj?
qa.a: It makes Suraj uncomfortable enough to step back into the wall, even though Gautam is only chatting.

grounding: It shows a child learning that about an arm's length suits talking with friends while family can come closer, with gentle coaching.
